title: Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Controlled Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Many strong models still fall well short on the task, but adding our inference method consistently improves every model it is applied to.

description: Two side-by-side scatter plots. The left panel plots Pearson r (x) against QWK (y), with higher values better. The right panel plots RMSE (x) against MAE (y), with lower values better. Each dot is one LLM, coloured by model and sized by parameter scale. Boxed, colour-coded callouts with leader lines highlight a few models, each shown with and without the MABGr. method: Gemini 3 Pro, DS-v4 Flash, Kimi K2.5 and Qwen3.5 27B. abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.
